t: Number of Orders in the Backlog: Order Matching with Two Heaps
o: Orders arrive as batches: orders[i] = [price, amount, type], where type 0 is a batch of buy units and type 1 a batch of sell units. A buy batch executes immediately against backlog sell orders cheapest-first while the best remaining sell price is <= the buy price; symmetrically, a sell batch consumes the most expensive backlog buys priced >= it. Whatever cannot execute waits in the backlog, and we must return the total leftover amount modulo 10^9 + 7. Trace orders = [[10,5,0],[15,5,1],[16,4,0]]: nothing can match the first batch, so 5 buys wait at price 10; the sell batch of 5 at 15 finds no backlog buy >= 15 and waits; the buy batch of 4 at 16 matches the cheapest sells at 15, executes all 4 units, leaving 1 sell unit at 15 — the backlog totals 5 + 1 = 6. With up to 10^5 batches, prices and amounts up to 10^9, repeatedly rescanning the books is far too slow; two priority queues expose exactly the extremes each match needs.
k: Buys consume the cheapest sells priced <= them and sells consume the priciest buys priced >= them — both sides always trade against the opposite extreme of the book.
Batches behave like stacks of identical orders: partial execution merely shrinks a batch, and any remainder re-enters its own heap.
A max-heap keyed by price for buys plus a min-heap for sells makes every execution step O(log n).
Leftover amounts can sum to about 10^14, so accumulate in a 64-bit integer before applying the final modulo.

a.i: Represent both books as plain lists of [price, amount] pairs. For each incoming batch, repeatedly scan the opposite list for the best-priced executable entry, trade off min(incoming, matched) units, drop exhausted entries, and stop when no candidate qualifies or the batch is spent; append any remainder to its own book. This mirrors the rules verbatim and is easy to trust, but quadratic behavior limits it to small inputs.
s: Maintain lists buy and sell of [price, amount] entries.
For an incoming buy batch, repeatedly locate the minimum-price sell with price <= buyPrice (for sells, the maximum-price buy with price >= sellPrice).
Execute min(incoming amount, matched amount) units and shrink both sides accordingly, removing the matched entry if it empties.
Stop matching when the batch is exhausted or no executable entry exists, then push the remainder onto its own book.
Sum all amounts across both books and reduce modulo 10^9 + 7.
a.t: O(n * B * L) — each match step scans the whole opposite book and removals shift arrays, degrading toward O(n^2) on adversarial inputs.
a.sp: O(n) for the two book lists.

a.n: Approach 2: Max-Heap for Buys, Min-Heap for Sells
a.i: Keep a max-heap of buy batches ordered by price and a min-heap of sell batches ordered by price, each entry holding [price, amount]. An incoming buy repeatedly inspects the cheapest sell: while that price is <= the buy price they trade min(units), shrinking or popping the top; leftovers of the incoming batch are pushed onto the buy heap afterward, and vice versa for sells. Each batch is pushed once and popped once per partial execution, so the total work is bounded by heap operations.
s: Create buyMax (priority by descending price) and sellMin (ascending price), entries of [price, amount].
For a buy batch: while amount remains and the cheapest sell has price <= buyPrice, execute min(amount, topAmount) units, popping the sell if it empties; push the unspent remainder into buyMax.
Mirror the logic for a sell batch against buyMax's most expensive buys.
Finally sum the amounts in both heaps modulo 10^9 + 7.
a.t: O(n log n) — each batch causes pushes and pops costing logarithmic time, and there are O(n) batches with at most O(n) total pops.
a.sp: O(n) — every unmatched batch occupies exactly one heap slot.

w: Go straight to the two-heaps design after sketching the simulation: interviewers expect it, and the brute force exists mainly to validate small cases. Pitfalls: mixing up the boundary comparisons (a buy matches sells at equal price, so <= and >=, not strict inequalities), pushing the remainder of the incoming batch back with its own key rather than the counterparty's, forgetting Python's negated keys for max-heaps, and truncating the answer by summing in 32-bit ints before the modulo. Edge cases: a single order that never matches, batches larger than the entire opposite book, and equal prices across many batches. Follow-up: supporting order cancellation or querying the best bid/ask at any moment maps naturally onto TreeMaps / multiset-backed books with the same asymptotics.
